claims.text: Heat-treatment-induced short-range chemical ordering in chromium-rich steels promotes localized chromium segregation.
Localized chromium segregation enables formation of a more uniform and protective chromium oxide film.
A more uniform protective chromium oxide film enhances corrosion resistance in aggressive chemical and nuclear environments.
Homogenized chromium-containing steel has a relatively random chromium distribution or L11-like ordering tendencies.
L11-like ordering is less effective than L12-like ordering at driving near-surface chromium segregation.
Heat treatment can promote L12-type short-range ordering.
L12-type short-range ordering encourages chromium clustering in the near-surface region of steel.
L12-like nanoclusters localize chromium atoms near the surface.
CrCoNi alloys exhibit L12 and L11 types of short-range order within nanoclusters.
In CrCoNi, L11 short-range order predominates in the homogenized state, whereas heat treatment promotes L12 formation.
Increasing the local chromium concentration at the surface facilitates formation and stabilization of a protective chromium oxide film.
The protective chromium oxide film impedes corrosion.
Heat-treated steels with increased L12-like order will have lower corrosion rates than homogenized steels.
Heat-treated steels with increased L12-like order will have more uniform oxide films and less pitting than homogenized steels.
A random or L11-dominated homogenized baseline has inferior chromium segregation, a less protective oxide layer, and a higher corrosion rate.
The proposed mechanism applies only where chromium-containing steels thermodynamically support passive-film formation.
The mechanism may fail at low chromium content, when the oxide film is unstable, or when other alloying elements dominate corrosion behavior.
